Watching exceptions as they happen

TracePoint (see Reflection, Introspection and Tracing) has a :raise event, fired when an exception is raised, and a :rescue event (Ruby 3.3, Ruby-level rescue only), fired when one is handled. It is the right tool for "who raises this and who swallows it" in a codebase that handles too much. tp.raised_exception is the exception object and tp.lineno and tp.path the location. The event is also fired for exceptions that Ruby’s own code raises and rescues internally, so filter on tp.path in real use.

# frozen_string_literal: true

def parse(text)
  raise ArgumentError, "not a number: #{text}" unless text.match?(/\A\d+\z/)

  text.to_i
end

def total(values) = values.sum { |text| parse(text) }

events = []
trace = TracePoint.new(:raise, :rescue) do |tp|
  events << [tp.event, tp.raised_exception.class, tp.lineno]
end

trace.enable do
  total(%w[1 two 3])
rescue ArgumentError
  events << :handled
end

events.each { |event| p event }
[:raise, ArgumentError, 4]
[:rescue, ArgumentError, 19]
:handled

Source: TracePoint

Warnings

Not every problem is an exception. warn writes to standard error and Warning controls which categories of interpreter warnings are shown:

  • Warning[:deprecated] is off by default (since Ruby 2.7.2), Warning[:experimental] is on, Warning[:performance] is off. Warning.categories lists the categories: :deprecated, :experimental, :performance and :strict_unused_block (the last two since 3.3 and 3.4).

  • ruby -w and ruby -W:deprecated (or -W:no-experimental) set them from the command line, and $VERBOSE set to nil silences warn as well.

  • warn "message", uplevel: 1, category: :deprecated reports the line of the caller (the uplevel keyword) and respects the category switch. This is the pattern for deprecating your own API. The example below is run without -w, which would switch the deprecated category on from the start.

  • Warning.warn is the single hook through which every warning passes. Prepending a module to its singleton class captures or reroutes them, for example into a logger or into a test failure (Ruby 3.0 added the category: keyword).

# frozen_string_literal: true

p Warning.categories
p Warning[:deprecated], Warning[:experimental], Warning[:performance]

def old_api
  warn "old_api is deprecated, use new_api", uplevel: 1, category: :deprecated
  :result
end

# Deprecation warnings are off by default; enabling the category shows them.
old_api
Warning[:deprecated] = true
old_api

# Route warnings somewhere else by overriding Warning.warn.
captured = []
Warning.singleton_class.prepend(Module.new do
  define_method(:warn) do |message, category: nil|
    captured << [category, message.chomp]
    nil
  end
end)

warn "captured by the hook"
old_api
cleaned = captured.map { |category, message| [category, message.sub(/\A.*?: warning: /, "")] }
p cleaned
[:deprecated, :experimental, :performance, :strict_unused_block]
false
true
false
warnings_demo.rb:14: warning: old_api is deprecated, use new_api
[[nil, "captured by the hook"], [:deprecated, "old_api is deprecated, use new_api"]]

Source: Kernel#warn

Source: Warning

Wrapping and chaining

When a low-level error crosses a layer boundary, wrap it in the error type of the layer it enters, so callers depend on the library’s errors and not on its implementation (Errno::ENOENT or a JSON::ParserError), and keep the original as the cause. Ruby does the second part for you: an exception raised inside a rescue clause automatically gets the exception being handled ($!) as its cause, since Ruby 2.1. Set cause: explicitly to attach a different one, or cause: nil to hide the implicit one when the original adds nothing.

The uncaught-exception printer and full_message show the whole chain, innermost cause last, as the second half of this example demonstrates (the script ends with an uncaught exception, so the printed report is the real standard error output):

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "shelf"

module Shelf
  class StoreError < Error; end

  # Wraps whatever the storage layer raises, keeping the original as cause.
  class FileStore
    def initialize(path) = @path = path

    def load
      File.read(@path)
    rescue SystemCallError
      raise StoreError, "cannot load catalogue from #{@path}"
    end
  end
end

store = Shelf::FileStore.new("catalogue.json")

begin
  store.load
rescue Shelf::StoreError => e
  puts "error:   #{e.message}"
  puts "cause:   #{e.cause.inspect}"
  chain = [e]
  chain << chain.last.cause while chain.last.cause
  puts "chain:   #{chain.map(&:class).join(' <- ')}"
end

# Uncaught, the whole chain is printed.
store.load
error:   cannot load catalogue from catalogue.json
cause:   #<Errno::ENOENT: No such file or directory @ rb_sysopen - catalogue.json>
chain:   Shelf::StoreError <- Errno::ENOENT
wrap_cause.rb:15:in 'Shelf::FileStore#load': cannot load catalogue from catalogue.json (Shelf::StoreError)
	from wrap_cause.rb:33:in '<main>'
wrap_cause.rb:13:in 'IO.read': No such file or directory @ rb_sysopen - catalogue.json (Errno::ENOENT)
	from wrap_cause.rb:13:in 'Shelf::FileStore#load'
	from wrap_cause.rb:33:in '<main>'

Source: Exception#cause

detailed_message shows only the exception itself; use full_message or walk cause to include the chain. A cause is a link in a singly linked list, so a loop such as chain << chain.last.cause while chain.last.cause is enough to collect it. Wrap deliberately: a wrapper that discards the original message (raise Shelf::StoreError) forces the reader to find the cause in a different place, so the wrapper’s message should say what the layer was doing, and the cause says why it failed.

Exceptions and control flow

An exception is the wrong tool for something that happens in normal operation. A missing hash key, a number that may not parse, a search that finds nothing: these have return values. Ruby gives most of the core methods both forms, so choose by whether the failure is expected:

When absence or failure is expected When it is a bug or an environmental fault

Integer(text, exception: false), Float(text, exception: false) return nil.

Integer(text) raises ArgumentError.

hash.fetch(key, default), hash.fetch(key) { block }, hash[key].

hash.fetch(key) raises KeyError.

array.find { } returns nil; find(ifnone) computes a default.

A method that must find something and raises when it cannot, conventionally named with ! or fetch.

The safe navigation operator &., Hash#dig, Array#first.

NoMethodError on nil.

catch/throw to leave nested loops.

raise for a real failure.

catch and throw (with break, next, return and redo, in Control Expressions) implement non-local exits that are not errors. throw tag, value unwinds the stack to the nearest catch(tag) with the same tag (compared by identity; symbols are conventional) and makes catch return the value. Without a matching catch, throw raises UncaughtThrowError, a subclass of ArgumentError that carries tag and value. loop rescues StopIteration for you and returns the iterator’s result, which is what makes loop { enum.next } a safe way to walk an enumerator.

# frozen_string_literal: true

# 1. Expected absence is a value, not an exception.
p Integer("12", exception: false)
p Integer("twelve", exception: false)
p Float("1.5x", exception: false)
catalog = { "9780306406157" => "Ruby Basics" }
p catalog.fetch("0000000000000", "unknown")
p catalog.fetch("0000000000000") { |isbn| "no title for #{isbn}" }
begin
  catalog.fetch("0000000000000")
rescue KeyError => e
  puts "#{e.message} (key: #{e.key.inspect})"
end

# 2. catch/throw leaves nested loops without an exception class of its own.
shelves = [%w[a b c], %w[d target f], %w[g h i]]
found = catch(:found) do
  shelves.each_with_index do |shelf, row|
    shelf.each_with_index do |title, col|
      throw :found, [row, col] if title == "target"
    end
  end
  nil
end
p found

# throw without a matching catch is an UncaughtThrowError (an ArgumentError).
begin
  throw :missing, 42
rescue UncaughtThrowError => e
  puts "#{e.message}; tag=#{e.tag.inspect} value=#{e.value}"
end

# 3. loop rescues StopIteration and returns the enumerator's result.
numbers = [10, 20].each
result = loop do
  puts numbers.next
end
p result

# 4. Searching: find returns nil, find with an ifnone lambda computes a default.
titles = ["Ruby Basics", "Rust Basics"]
missing = titles.find { it.start_with?("Go") }
fallback = titles.find(-> { "none" }) { it.start_with?("Go") }
p missing, fallback
12
nil
nil
"unknown"
"no title for 0000000000000"
key not found: "0000000000000" (key: "0000000000000")
[1, 1]
uncaught throw :missing; tag=:missing value=42
10
20
[10, 20]
nil
"none"

Source: Kernel#catch

Source: Kernel#throw, Kernel#Integer, Kernel#loop

Two further reasons not to use exceptions for ordinary branching: creating one captures a backtrace, which costs far more than returning a value, and it makes the happy path unreadable because the reader must look for the rescue far from the call. Lint/SuppressedExceptionInNumberConversion goes after the most common abuse, Integer(text) rescue 0.

Fail fast or recover

The decision a handler makes, in order:

  1. Can this code repair the situation? A missing optional file can fall back to defaults; a transient network failure can be retried with backoff. Then rescue the specific class, repair, and continue.

  2. Can it add context and pass it on? Wrap into the layer’s own error with cause, or add a message with raise error, "more context", and let the caller decide.

  3. Neither? Do not rescue. Let the exception travel to the one place at the edge of the program that reports and exits.

Failing fast means raising at the first sign of an invalid state (a precondition on an argument, an invariant of a value object) rather than letting a nil travel three layers and fail with a confusing NoMethodError. Shelf::Isbn.new does this: an invalid ISBN never becomes an object.

Timeouts

Timeout.timeout(seconds) { ... } from the timeout default gem (require "timeout") interrupts the block when the time is up. It is simple, and its limits matter:

  • The interruption is an exception injected into the thread at an arbitrary point. Inside the block, Ruby code that is running at that moment is interrupted wherever it happens to be, including in the middle of updating a data structure.

  • To stop the block’s own rescue => e from swallowing the timeout, Ruby raises Timeout::ExitException, an Exception, inside the block and converts it into Timeout::Error (a RuntimeError) at the Timeout.timeout call. If you pass your own class as the second argument (Timeout.timeout(5, Shelf::StoreError, "store too slow")), that class is raised inside the block as is, and a rescue StandardError in the block can catch it.

  • ensure clauses in the block run, and can themselves be interrupted. The documentation recommends putting the Timeout.timeout call inside a begin/ensure rather than the other way round, and Thread.handle_interrupt for the hard cases.

  • A block can defeat the timeout by rescuing the exception or by never reaching a point where the interruption is delivered, so the method "cannot be relied on to enforce timeouts for untrusted blocks".

  • 0 and nil mean "no limit"; a negative number is an ArgumentError (Ruby 3.4).

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "timeout"

class SlowStoreError < StandardError; end

# Finishes in time: returns the block's value.
p Timeout.timeout(1) { :fast }

# Expires: Timeout::Error, a RuntimeError, raised where the call started.
begin
  Timeout.timeout(0.05) { sleep }
rescue Timeout::Error => e
  puts "#{e.class}: #{e.message}"
  p Timeout::Error.ancestors.take(3)
end

# The exception that interrupts the block is Timeout::ExitException, an
# Exception, so the block's own `rescue => e` cannot swallow it.
begin
  Timeout.timeout(0.05) do
    sleep
  rescue StandardError
    puts "never printed"
  ensure
    puts "ensure still runs"
  end
rescue Timeout::Error => e
  puts "outside: #{e.class}"
end

# A custom class and message are raised at the interrupted point instead.
begin
  Timeout.timeout(0.05, SlowStoreError, "store too slow") { sleep }
rescue SlowStoreError => e
  puts "#{e.class}: #{e.message}"
end

# nil and 0 mean no limit; a negative limit is rejected.
p Timeout.timeout(nil) { :unlimited }
begin
  Timeout.timeout(-1) { :never }
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts e.message
end

# The reliable alternative is a timeout on the operation itself.
r, = IO.pipe
r.timeout = 0.05
begin
  r.read(1)
rescue IO::TimeoutError => e
  puts "#{e.class}: #{e.message}"
end
:fast
Timeout::Error: execution expired
[Timeout::Error, RuntimeError, StandardError]
ensure still runs
outside: Timeout::Error
SlowStoreError: store too slow
:unlimited
Timeout sec must be a non-negative number
IO::TimeoutError: Blocking operation timed out!

Source: Timeout.timeout

Source: Timeout, IO#timeout=

Where the operation itself offers a timeout, use that instead: it fails at a well-defined point and without interrupting arbitrary code. IO#timeout= makes blocking reads and writes raise IO::TimeoutError (Ruby 3.2), Thread::Queue#pop(timeout:) returns nil (3.2), Regexp.timeout= bounds a match (3.2), Socket.tcp and TCPSocket.new accept open_timeout: and raise IO::TimeoutError consistently (4.0), and Net::HTTP has open_timeout, read_timeout and write_timeout (see Networking and HTTP). A fiber scheduler can implement timeout_after, which makes Timeout.timeout non-blocking (3.1).

Exceptions in threads, fibers and ractors

An exception that is not rescued in a thread ends that thread only. The main thread is not told until it asks: Thread#join and Thread#value re-raise the exception in the caller. Meanwhile the interpreter prints a report to standard error when the thread dies (Thread.report_on_exception, true by default since Ruby 2.5, settable per thread), and Thread.abort_on_exception = true turns any thread’s failure into an exception in the main thread, which is convenient for scripts and wrong for servers.

Thread#raise injects an exception into another thread, the same mechanism that Timeout uses; since Ruby 4.0 it accepts cause: like Kernel#raise, and so does Fiber#raise. In a fiber, an unrescued exception propagates to whoever called resume. In a ractor, an exception ends the ractor and is delivered to the caller as Ractor::RemoteError with the original as its cause. The concurrency pages go deeper: Threads and the GVL, Fibers and the Fiber Scheduler and Ractors.

# frozen_string_literal: true

Thread.report_on_exception = false

worker = Thread.new { Integer("not a number") }
begin
  worker.join
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts "join re-raised: #{e.message}"
end

begin
  Thread.new { raise IOError, "disk gone" }.value
rescue IOError => e
  puts "value re-raised: #{e.message}"
end
puts "status of a failed thread: #{worker.status.inspect}"

# Thread#raise injects an exception into another thread.
sleeper = Thread.new do
  sleep
rescue Interrupt => e
  "woken by #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
end
Thread.pass until sleeper.status == "sleep"
sleeper.raise(Interrupt, "wake up")
puts sleeper.value

# Since 4.0 the injected exception can carry its own cause.
t = Thread.new { sleep }
Thread.pass until t.status == "sleep"
t.raise(RuntimeError, "stop", cause: ArgumentError.new("because"))
begin
  t.join
rescue RuntimeError => e
  puts "#{e.message} <- #{e.cause.message}"
end
join re-raised: invalid value for Integer(): "not a number"
value re-raised: disk gone
status of a failed thread: nil
woken by Interrupt: wake up
stop <- because

Source: Thread

Source: Thread.report_on_exception, ThreadError

Ending the program

A Ruby program ends in one of four ways, each with a different exit status and different cleanup:

How Status What runs

Falling off the end of the script

0

at_exit handlers, in reverse registration order (the last registered runs first), then finalizers.

exit, exit(true), exit(false), exit(n)

0, 0, 1, n

Raises SystemExit; ensure clauses on the way up run; then at_exit handlers. SystemExit#status and #success? expose the status; rescue SystemExit stops it.

abort("message")

1

Prints the message to standard error, then behaves like exit(false).

An uncaught exception

1

ensure clauses while the exception unwinds, then the at_exit handlers, and only then the report (full_message with the cause chain) on standard error.

exit!

1 by default, or the given status

Ends the process immediately: no ensure, no at_exit, no flushing of Ruby’s buffers. For forked children that must not run the parent’s handlers.

An exit inside an at_exit handler changes the final status. END { } is a keyword form of at_exit that registers once (RuboCop’s Style/EndBlock asks for at_exit). Signals reach Ruby as exceptions in the main thread: Ctrl-C raises Interrupt (a SignalException with signo 2) and kill -TERM raises SignalException SIGTERM; handlers installed with Signal.trap replace that behaviour (see Processes, Signals and Shell).

The following program starts a child Ruby process for each ending and prints its status and output, so the cleanup behaviour is visible:

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "English"
require "rbconfig"

# Each child process shows one way a Ruby program ends.
CHILDREN = {
  "normal end" => "puts 'done'",
  "exit" => "exit",
  "exit(false)" => "exit(false)",
  "exit 3" => "exit 3",
  "abort" => "abort 'fatal: catalogue corrupt'",
  "uncaught raise" => "raise 'boom'",
  "rescued SystemExit" => <<~'RUBY'.tr("\n", ";"),
    begin
      exit 9
    rescue SystemExit => e
      puts "rescued status=#{e.status}"
    end
  RUBY
  "ensure and at_exit" => <<~RUBY.tr("\n", ";"),
    at_exit { puts 'at_exit 1' }
    at_exit { puts 'at_exit 2' }
    begin
      exit 4
    ensure
      puts 'ensure'
    end
  RUBY
  "exit!" => <<~RUBY.tr("\n", ";")
    at_exit { puts 'skipped' }
    begin
      exit! 5
    ensure
      puts 'skipped too'
    end
  RUBY
}.freeze

CHILDREN.each do |label, code|
  output = IO.popen([RbConfig.ruby, "-e", code, { err: %i[child out] }], &:read)
  puts "#{label}: status=#{$CHILD_STATUS.exitstatus}"
  output.each_line { |line| puts "    #{line}" }
end
normal end: status=0
    done
exit: status=0
exit(false): status=1
exit 3: status=3
abort: status=1
    fatal: catalogue corrupt
uncaught raise: status=1
    -e:1:in '<main>': boom (RuntimeError)
rescued SystemExit: status=0
    rescued status=9
ensure and at_exit: status=4
    ensure
    at_exit 2
    at_exit 1
exit!: status=5

Source: Kernel#exit

Source: Kernel#abort, Kernel#at_exit, SystemExit

Interrupt handling in a script follows from the table. A program that has resources to release should rely on ensure, which runs for Interrupt and SystemExit too, and should not rescue Interrupt unless it has something to say:

# frozen_string_literal: true

# Ctrl-C arrives as an Interrupt raised in the main thread.
begin
  Process.kill("INT", Process.pid)
  sleep
rescue Interrupt => e
  puts "#{e.class} (a #{e.class.superclass}), message #{e.message.inspect}, signo #{e.signo}"
end

# Other signals arrive as a plain SignalException.
begin
  Process.kill("TERM", Process.pid)
  sleep
rescue SignalException => e
  puts "#{e.signm} (#{e.signo})"
end
Interrupt (a SignalException), message "", signo 2
SIGTERM (15)

Source: Interrupt

Source: SignalException

Handling errors at the edge of a program

Libraries raise; the program decides. In a command-line program, a service or a background job there is one place, the outermost method, that knows what a failure means for the user and the process: print a message, choose an exit status, log with the right severity, and perhaps retry the job. Everything below it just raises, and a rescue below it is justified only when it repairs or wraps.

The example is the shape most scripts want: a main that returns an exit status, a table that maps error classes to statuses (the values follow the BSD sysexits.h convention: 64 usage, 65 bad data, 70 internal error), a Logger rather than puts for diagnostics (severity, destination and format are configurable, and they go to standard error, not standard output, so the program’s output can be piped), and a single exit in the script body. The logger library is a bundled gem since Ruby 4.0, so a project that runs under Bundler needs gem "logger" in its Gemfile.

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "logger"
require "shelf"

LOGGER = Logger.new($stderr, formatter: proc { |severity, _time, _prog, message| "#{severity}: #{message}\n" })

module Shelf
  class UsageError < Error; end
end

# Exit statuses follow sysexits.h: 64 usage, 65 bad data, 70 internal error.
STATUS = { Shelf::UsageError => 64, ArgumentError => 65 }.freeze

def run(argv)
  raise Shelf::UsageError, "usage: shelf ISBN" if argv.empty?

  puts Shelf::Isbn.new(argv.first)
end

# One place decides how failures are reported and which status the process
# returns; everything below it just raises.
def main(argv)
  run(argv)
  0
rescue Shelf::Error, ArgumentError => e
  LOGGER.warn("#{e.class}: #{e.message}")
  STATUS.fetch(e.class, 64)
rescue StandardError => e
  LOGGER.error("#{e.class}: #{e.message}")
  70
end

[[], ["123"], ["978-0-306-40615-7"]].each do |argv|
  puts "status #{main(argv)}"
end
WARN: Shelf::UsageError: usage: shelf ISBN
status 64
WARN: ArgumentError: invalid ISBN: 123
status 65
9780306406157
status 0

Source: Kernel#exit

Command-line details such as OptionParser error classes and exit status conventions are in Command-Line Programs. For network code, remember that the errors worth rescuing from Net::HTTP are the transport errors (SocketError, Errno::ECONNREFUSED, Timeout::Error/Net::OpenTimeout/Net::ReadTimeout, OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError, EOFError), which are not subclasses of any Net::HTTP error class; a rescue Net::HTTPError handler written from an older tutorial misses them. That list lives with the HTTP client in Networking and HTTP.

Testing error paths

An error path that is not tested is a guess. Minitest’s assert_raises(Klass) { ... } passes when the block raises Klass or a subclass, fails when it raises nothing or something else, and returns the exception so that the message, the cause or the extra data can be asserted. RSpec’s equivalent is expect { ... }.to raise_error(Klass, message); see Testing with Minitest and RSpec and Test Doubles. Test the class and the data, and test the message with care: asserting an exact message ties the test to wording, and messages of core classes change between Ruby versions (see the version notes below).

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "minitest/autorun"
require "shelf"

class IsbnErrorsTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_rejects_short_isbn
    error = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { Shelf::Isbn.new("978") }
    assert_equal "invalid ISBN: 978", error.message
  end

  def test_subclass_is_accepted
    assert_raises(StandardError) { Shelf::Isbn.new("978") }
  end

  def test_valid_isbn_does_not_raise
    assert_equal "9780306406157", Shelf::Isbn.new("978-0-306-40615-7").digits
  end
end
3 runs, 4 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips

Source: Minitest

(The output shows only the summary line of the run; Minitest also prints a random seed and the elapsed time.) minitest is a bundled gem in Ruby 4.0 (version 6.0.0): a project under Bundler lists it in its Gemfile.

Guidelines

The practices that the sections above justify, as a checklist:

  • Rescue the narrowest class that names the failure you can handle. rescue StandardError is acceptable only at a boundary, and rescue Exception almost never.

  • Keep the begin body to the statements that can raise the handled exception; put the success path in else.

  • Never leave a rescue clause empty. If an error is deliberately ignored, say why in a comment (RuboCop’s Lint/SuppressedException accepts a commented empty clause) or use a method that has a failure-free form.

  • Handle each failure once, at the layer that can act on it; wrap with cause when crossing layers; log at the edge.

  • Use ensure, or better a block form, for cleanup; never return from ensure.

  • Define a root error per library and subclass it; carry data in readers; do not parse messages.

  • Retry only transient, idempotent operations, with a limit and growing delays; never retry programming errors.

  • Prefer return values (exception: false, fetch with a default, find) for expected absence.

  • Put timeouts on the operation (IO#timeout=, HTTP client options) rather than around arbitrary code.

  • Test the error paths, and assert_raises the class and the data, not the wording.

RuboCop cops for exceptions

RuboCop ships a family of cops that encode these rules. All of them are enabled by default (the NewCops: enable setting used by the shelf configuration turns on the cops that are new in each release too).

Cop What it reports

Lint/RescueException

rescue Exception.

Style/RescueStandardError

A bare rescue (style explicit: write rescue StandardError). The implicit style does the opposite.

Lint/SuppressedException

An empty rescue clause (a comment inside is accepted by default).

Lint/SuppressedExceptionInNumberConversion

Integer(x) rescue nil and friends: use exception: false.

Style/RescueModifier

expression rescue fallback.

Lint/ShadowedException

A rescue clause listing a class after its superclass, which can never be reached.

Lint/DuplicateRescueException

The same class listed twice.

Lint/RescueType

A rescue with something that is not a class or module, such as a string.

Lint/EnsureReturn

return inside ensure.

Lint/EmptyEnsure and Lint/UselessRescue

An empty ensure, and a rescue that only re-raises.

Style/RedundantBegin

A begin block that a method body would make unnecessary.

Style/SignalException

fail (the default style only_raise requires raise).

Style/RaiseArgs

raise Klass.new("message") when raise Klass, "message" is enough.

Style/RedundantException

raise RuntimeError, "message" where raise "message" is equivalent.

Lint/RaiseException and Lint/InheritException

raise Exception and class MyError < Exception.

Layout/RescueEnsureAlignment

A rescue or ensure not aligned with its begin or def.

See Style, Linting and Static Analysis for configuring and running RuboCop.

Pitfalls

  • rescue Exception swallows exit and Ctrl-C. A script that cannot be interrupted usually has one.

  • raise Klass, key: value does not call the constructor with a keyword. The keywords become the message. Raise an object: raise Klass.new(...).

  • Exceptions in else, ensure and rescue are not seen by the sibling rescue clauses. Nest a begin if needed.

  • return in ensure hides the exception in flight.

  • A rescue entry that is not a class (a string, a method that returned nil) raises TypeError when an exception arrives, and hides it.

  • NotImplementedError is not rescued by a bare rescue.

  • retry without a limit is an infinite loop for a permanent failure.

  • Timeout.timeout can interrupt anything, including cleanup. Use the operation’s own timeout.

  • Thread.abort_on_exception = true in a library changes the behaviour of the whole process. Use report_on_exception and join.

  • $! outside a rescue clause is nil, and inside it can change when another exception is handled in between. Use the variable of rescue => e.

  • Error messages that include secrets (passwords, tokens, full URLs with credentials) end up in logs and error trackers. Include identifiers, not the data.

  • Matching on message text (e.message.include?("not found")) breaks when wording changes. Use classes and readers.

  • Rescuing NoMethodError to detect nil. Use &., a guard clause or a default; a rescued NoMethodError also hides typos.

  • A rescue in a brace block is a syntax error; use do/end.

  • Rescuing from a hot loop. Raising captures a backtrace; return a value in code that runs often.

Comparison with other languages

Language Model Difference from Ruby

Java

try/catch/finally, checked and unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources.

Ruby has no checked exceptions and no throws; ensure replaces finally, and a block form replaces try-with-resources.

Python

try/except/else/finally, raise ... from.

The closest model. Ruby’s cause is set implicitly, and a bare rescue is StandardError, like a bare except Exception.

Kotlin and C#

Unchecked exceptions, try is an expression (Kotlin).

Ruby’s begin is an expression too; there is no exception filter (when), but rescue accepts any object with ===.

Go and Rust

Errors are return values (error, Result).

Ruby returns values for expected absence (nil, exception: false) and raises for faults.

Swift

throws/try/catch, typed by protocol.

Swift makes every throwing call visible with try; Ruby does not.

Where the books are outdated or wrong

Older books and tutorials on Ruby error handling are still useful for the ideas, but several details have changed or were never right. Wherever a printed example differs from the output on this page, this table says why.

Area Older material shows Current approach (Ruby 4.0)

Error message format

undefined method `foo' for nil:NilClass, with a backtick and a class name.

undefined method 'foo' for nil (Ruby 3.3 receiver format, 3.4 apostrophe) and, for other objects, for an instance of Shelf::Isbn.

Backtrace labels

in `parse'.

in 'Object#parse', with the class (Ruby 3.4).

Hash in a message or inspect

{:name=>"Ico"}.

{name: "Ico"} and {"name" => "Ico"} (Ruby 3.4).

Abstract methods

raise NotImplementedError in the base class.

NotImplementedError is a ScriptError that a bare rescue does not catch. Raise NoMethodError or a project error.

Catch-all handling

rescue Exception => e as the general handler.

rescue StandardError, or a bare rescue. rescue Exception breaks exit, Ctrl-C and timeouts.

Wrapping errors

A plain Exception instance or subclass used as the wrapper, and a rescue of a class that is not defined in that scope.

A StandardError subclass with cause; the root error of the library.

Network errors

rescue Net::HTTPError around an HTTP call.

The transport errors (SocketError, Errno::*, Timeout::Error, OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError) are not Net::HTTP errors.

Logging

Logger described as part of the standard library.

logger is a bundled gem since Ruby 4.0: under Bundler it needs a Gemfile entry.

Printing order

Output headed "Traceback (most recent call last)", outermost frame first (an experiment of Ruby 2.5 to 2.7 on terminals).

Innermost first again since Ruby 3.0; full_message(order: :bottom) gives the reversed layout.

Cause

A custom attribute (original) to keep the wrapped error.

Exception#cause is set automatically (Ruby 2.1) and cause: overrides it.

Pattern-matching errors

Not covered.

NoMatchingPatternError and NoMatchingPatternKeyError for case/in and => with no match.

Version notes

Version Change

2.1

Exception#cause: the exception being handled is recorded automatically.

2.5

rescue, else and ensure allowed directly in do/end blocks. Exception#full_message. FrozenError. KeyError#key and #receiver. Thread.report_on_exception defaults to true. An experimental reverse-order error printer on terminals (undone in 3.0).

3.0

The error printer shows the innermost frame first. --backtrace-limit. Warning.warn accepts category:.

3.1

error_highlight ships with Ruby. Class#subclasses. Timeout.timeout is non-blocking under a fiber scheduler. Thread::Backtrace.limit.

3.2

Exception#detailed_message; the error printer calls it. IO#timeout= and IO::TimeoutError. Regexp.timeout=. Thread::Queue#pop(timeout:). Control characters are no longer escaped in error messages.

3.3

NoMethodError messages say for an instance of ClassName instead of calling inspect. TracePoint :rescue event. A :performance warning category.

3.4

Error messages and backtraces use an apostrophe instead of a backtick, and method labels include the class. Extra rescue and ensure frames are gone from backtraces. Exception#set_backtrace, Kernel#raise, Thread#raise and Fiber#raise accept arrays of Thread::Backtrace::Location. Warning.categories. Negative Timeout.timeout values are rejected. Hash#inspect format changed.

4.0

error_highlight shows caller and callee snippets for ArgumentError about arity. Thread#raise(cause:) and Fiber#raise(cause:). Backtraces no longer show internal frames of core methods written in Ruby; the backtrace of an arity ArgumentError names the class. TCPSocket.new and Socket.tcp raise IO::TimeoutError consistently and accept open_timeout:. logger and minitest are bundled gems.
